_comment: Flagship Lithuanian and Latvian legends (Egle the Serpent Queen, Laczplesis, the Iron Wolf of Gediminas, Kurbads) retold from the documented folk tradition; based on Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979), Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992), Gimbutas, The Balts (1963), Ruke-Dravina's Latvian collections, and the Laczplesis epic of Andrejs Pumpurs (1888). All passages paraphrase.

title.en: Egle and the Serpent King: The Marriage Beneath the River
title.zh: 埃格萊與蛇王：河底之婚

region.en: Riverside fields, Lithuania (symbolic pin at Kaunas)
region.zh: 立陶宛河畔田野（象徵性定位於考納斯）

texts.period: Folk tale recorded 19th c.; documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

source.work: Lithuanian folk tale 'Egle zalcio karaliene' (Egle, Queen of the Serpents); as documented in N. Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979) and A. J. Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Egle, washing her family's linen, finds a serpent in her sleeve; he will give it back only for a promise of marriage. Her brothers-in-law substitute a goose, and later a heifer — but the third time the snake-king Zilvinas rings the wedding bell himself and carries his true bride down into the crystal palace beneath the river.
summary.zh: 埃格萊浣衣時袖中得一蛇；蛇索婚約方肯歸還。三位兄嫂代嫁鵝、再代嫁牛——第三次，蛇王日爾維納斯親鳴婚鐘，攜真正新娘降至河底水晶宮。

sensitivity.note: Lithuania's national folktale; its imagery is public cultural property, retold without community restriction.

passages.text: Egle, the youngest of a family's daughters, washes the household linen by the river; when she shakes out her sleeves a serpent tumbles from the folds and asks her promise of marriage as the price of the clothing. Egle laughs and promises — and when the family cannot believe it, the serpent king sends his kin to claim his bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lithuanian tale as documented in Vellius, Lithuanian Mythological Tales (1979), and Greimas, Of Gods and Men (1992); not verbatim.

passages.text: The eldest brother-in-law dresses a goose in bridal linen; the serpents ring it about the riverbank and the goose's honking betrays the cheat. A second substitution — a black heifer this time — is unmasked the same way: lowing instead of speaking. On the third attempt the family gives up Egle herself; the serpent king Zilvinas rings his wedding-bell, and the waters open a road down to a palace of crystal where the wedding feast is already laid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tale; not verbatim.

title.en: The Axe Against the Willow: Egle's Brothers-in-Law
title.zh: 斫柳之斧：埃格萊的兄長們

region.zh: 立陶宛河畔（象徵性定位於考納斯）

texts.period: Folk tale recorded 19th c.; documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

source.work: Lithuanian folk tale 'Egle zalcio karaliene', second movement; documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: In the underwater kingdom Egle bears three sons and a daughter and lives happily until she longs for home; Zilvinas lets her visit — but first the brothers-in-law must go to the oak: three are loyal, and one takes the axe to the living willow that holds Zilvinas's life.
summary.zh: 河底王國中埃格萊育三子一女，幸福美滿；思鄉之際，日爾維納斯許其探親——但先須至橡樹前誓：三個忠誠，一個却持斧斫向藏日爾維納斯性命之活柳。

sensitivity.note: External-soul motif (willow holding the serpent king's life).

passages.text: In the crystal palace under the river Egle lives in happiness, and in time her three sons and her daughter grow tall about her. Still the heart longs for its mother's door, and Egle asks Zilvinas for a visit. He grants it — but first he sends her brothers-in-law to the old oak with a scythe and a question: what is Egle's husband's foe, and what would you do if you met him?
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tale in Vellius (1979), Greimas (1992); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two brothers answer faithfully: 'the fly is his foe; if I met him I would bristle and bite.' The third lies, and takes his revenge: at Zilvinas's order he goes to the willow — the living willow in which the serpent king keeps his life — and strikes it nine times with the axe. Each stroke, Zilvinas feels as his own blood: at the first he roars, at the third he bellows, at the ninth he is a corpse on the crystal floor, and the road home from the underwater kingdom closes behind Egle forever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tale; not verbatim.

title.en: Egle and the Four Reeds: Children Changed to Trees
title.zh: 埃格萊與四株蘆葦：子女化樹

region.zh: 立陶宛河畔（象徵性定位於考納斯）

texts.period: Folk tale recorded 19th c.; documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

source.work: Lithuanian folk tale 'Egle zalcio karaliene', final movement; documented in Vellius (1979) and Greimas (1992)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Ordered by the brothers to say where she would rather live, Egle calls her children — who answer by naming what they would become: an oak, an ash, a birch, and a juniper; at the river's edge she strikes the bank with her whip, and all four become trees at the shore while she becomes a spruce, forever green by the water where her serpent husband's palace stands.
summary.zh: 兄長令她言明更願居於何處；埃格萊喚子女——孩子們各自說出將化身何物：橡、白蠟、樺、檜；她在河岸揮鞭擊土，四子皆化為樹，她自化為雲杉，永綠於蛇夫水晶宮畔的水邊。

sensitivity.note: Closing of Lithuania's national tale; the transformed children are a byword for family grief.

passages.text: Egle lives with her children at the riverbank after Zilvinas's death; the brothers demand that she give up the children and marry among them, or say at once where she will live and with whom. Egle answers only by calling her children, and each names what he would rather be than a house of men: the eldest an oak, the second an ash, the daughter a birch, the youngest a juniper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tale in Vellius (1979), Greimas (1992); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Egle takes her whip, strikes the riverbank four times, and at each blow one of the children becomes the tree he has named — and Egle herself becomes the spruce, forever green beside the water, while beneath it the crystal palace of Zilvinas shines up through the current. The Lithuanians still point to waterside trees as the children of Egle; and the tale is told at every river where the spruce leans out over the water it will not leave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented tale; not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth of Laczplesis: The Bear's Ears
title.zh: 拉奇普萊西斯誕生：熊之耳

region.zh: 拉脫維亞庫爾澤梅（象徵性定位於庫爾迪加）

texts.period: Folk layers recorded in the Laczplesis epic of Andrejs Pumpurs (1888)

source.work: Andrejs Pumpurs, Lacplesis (1888), opening cantos, drawing on Latvian folk legend of the Bear-Slayer; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian collections and Gimbutas, The Balts (1963)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: A she-bear carries off a child to her den and suckles him; found as a boy wearing bear's ears, Laczplesis — the Bear-Slayer — kills the monstrous bear that devours the land's herds, and gains strength to grow whenever he touches the earth of his homeland.
summary.zh: 母熊擄嬰入穴哺育；被尋回時孩童戴熊耳，是為拉奇普萊西斯——『殺熊者』；他誅滅吞噬全境牛群之巨熊，且觸祖國大地即可增力。

sensitivity.note: Latvia's national hero of the epic cycle; symbolic of Latvian resistance.

passages.text: A child is carried off by a she-bear to her den among the rocks, and suckled among her cubs; the hunters who find him discover a boy wearing the bear's ears he cannot put off. He is named Laczplesis — the Bear-Slayer — and grows up herding and hunting in the Kurzeme forests with the strength of the wild beast that raised him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bear-Slayer legend as recorded in the folk layers of Pumpurs's Lacplesis epic (1888); not verbatim.

passages.text: A monstrous bear, older and stronger than any of the land, breaks out to devour the herds and the shepherds; Laczplesis wrestles it for a day and a night, tears off its ears, and wears them as his own; from that hour the people call him the Bear-Slayer, and the strength of the bear lives in him. Only one law binds him: his strength returns to him whenever he touches the earth of his homeland — the rock, the field, the riverbank of Latvia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the documented legend; not verbatim.

title.en: The Black Knight on the Daugava: The Fall of Laczplesis
title.zh: 道加瓦河畔的黑騎士：拉奇普萊西斯之殞

region.en: Castle by the Daugava, Latvia (symbolic pin at Koknese)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞道加瓦河畔古堡（象徵性定位於科克內塞）

texts.period: Recorded in the Lacplesis epic of Andrejs Pumpurs (1888)

source.work: Andrejs Pumpurs, Lacplesis (1888), closing cantos; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian collections

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: A black knight comes out of the German castle on the Daugava to challenge the land: he wears Laczplesis's own strength beneath his armour, for he is the giant's ear split from the bear-slayer's skin; thrown into the river by treachery — off the earth that gave him strength — Laczplesis falls, and the black knight's bridge of bones rises from the water.
summary.zh: 黑騎士自道加瓦河畔日耳曼城堡而出，向國土挑戰；其甲內藏著拉奇普萊西斯自己的力——原是熊皮之耳的巨妖；因奸計被拋入河、離開賜力之大地，拉奇普萊西斯殞落，黑騎士的白骨之橋自水中升起。

sensitivity.note: National epic fall; read symbolically as the loss of Latvian freedom under the German orders.

passages.text: At the castle on the Daugava a black knight rides out in armour and challenges the land to single combat; no Latvian hero can stand against him, for his power is strange. Laczplesis comes down to fight him and wins every fall — but the knight's secret is the bear-slayer's own strength: he is a being of the bear's ear, split from Laczplesis's skin, and every grip he makes draws the strength out of the hero's body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the closing cantos of Pumpurs's Lacplesis (1888); not verbatim.

passages.text: Treachery does what arms cannot: Laczplesis is flung from the bridge into the Daugava — off the earth that gave him strength — and drowns in the river he has always ruled. From the water rises the black knight's bridge, built of the bones of the fallen, and the land is held by strangers for seven hundred years. But the Latvians sing that the day of liberation is foretold by the Bear-Slayer's re-awakening — and when the bridge of bones breaks at last, Laczplesis himself will rise from the Daugava.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the closing cantos; not verbatim.

title.en: The Iron Wolf: Gediminas's Dream at Vilnius
title.zh: 鐵狼：格迪米納斯維爾紐斯之夢

region.en: Vilnius, Lithuania (symbolic pin at Vilnius castle hill)
region.zh: 立陶宛維爾紐斯（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯城堡山）

texts.period: Legend dated c. 1322-23; recorded in the Lithuanian chronicles (Bychowiec, 16th c.)

source.work: The Iron Wolf dream of Grand Duke Gediminas, from the Lithuanian (Bychowiec) chronicle tradition; documented in Gimbutas, The Balts (1963) and Greimas (1992)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain legend; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Hunting near the hills, Gediminas dreams a giant iron wolf on the hilltop howling as if a hundred wolves were inside it; the pagan priest Lizdeika interprets the dream — build the city here, for the howling wolf is the fame of a fortress whose renown will carry as far as the wolf's howl — and Vilnius is founded.
summary.zh: 圍獵山丘之際，格迪米納斯夢見山頂立一巨鐵狼，長嚎如體內藏百狼；異教祭司利茲傑伊卡釋夢——於此築城，狼嚎即城堡聲名遠揚之兆——維爾紐斯乃建。

sensitivity.note: Founding legend of Lithuania's capital; the wolf statue stands at the cathedral.

passages.text: Grand Duke Gediminas, hunting near the hills above the Vilnia, has killed an aurochs and sleeps: he dreams a giant wolf of iron standing on the hilltop, howling as though a hundred wolves were howling inside it. He wakes and asks the priest Lizdeika, the pagan high-priest of his fathers, what the dream means.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iron Wolf founding legend from the Lithuanian chronicle tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: Lizdeika answers: the iron wolf is a fortress — build it on this hill, and its fame will howl out through the world as the wolf's howl carried through the forest. Gediminas builds Vilnius, and the Iron Wolf's howl is the city's own: 'the iron wolf' became the emblem of the Lithuanian capital, whose statue of the wolf stands beside the cathedral to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the legend; not verbatim.

title.en: Kurbads: The Hero Born of the Bear
title.zh: 庫爾巴德斯：熊生之英雄

region.zh: 拉脫維亞維澤梅（象徵性定位於采西斯）

texts.period: Latvian hero cycle recorded 19th c.; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian collections

source.work: The Kurbads (Kurbads/Kurbat) hero cycle of Latvian folk legend; documented in V. Ruke-Dravina's Latvian tale collections and Gimbutas, The Balts (1963)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: The Latvian hero Kurbads, of the bear-born line of Laczplesis's kin, is found as a child in a den among bears; given to a poor family he grows with the strength of the wild wood, and sets out with the task of freeing the land from the robbers who rule it.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞英雄庫爾巴德斯——拉奇普萊西斯之族裔、熊之血統——幼時於熊穴被尋獲；寄養貧家，具林野之力；長而出發，解救受強盜轄制之國土。

passages.text: In the Latvian hero cycle Kurbads is a child found among bears in the dens of the forest — of the same miraculous family as the Bear-Slayer Laczplesis, fed on bear's milk and bear's strength. A childless family takes him in, and he grows up with the wildness of the wood in his limbs: whatever he touches, the strength of the bear is in his hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kurbads hero cycle as documented in Latvian collections (Ruke-Dravina; Gimbutas, The Balts); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sets out as a young man with the only work worth doing: to free the land of the monsters that hold its roads — the giants and dragons and three-headed robbers who steal harvests and brides. His mother gives him three loaves baked with her tears, and he walks out of the forest into the wide world where the Latvian heroes do their work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the cycle; not verbatim.

title.zh: 庫爾巴德斯與三首巨人

region.en: Vidzeme roads, Latvia (symbolic pin at Cesis)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞維澤梅道路（象徵性定位於采西斯）

texts.period: Latvian hero cycle recorded 19th c.; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian collections

source.work: The Kurbads hero cycle, the Three-Headed episode; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian tale collections

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: The three-headed giant with the iron staff holds the road; Kurbads serves him to win his sister, cuts the staff's strength away at the river, and beats the three heads at their own game — the three blacksmiths of the Latvian fields.
summary.zh: 持鐵杖之三首巨人霸佔道路；庫爾巴德斯為娶其妹而投效，於河畔斷其杖力，並以巨人自己的賭局反制三首——拉脫維亞田野上的三個鐵匠。

passages.text: On the road Kurbads meets the Three-Headed Giant, each head doing its own work: one eats, one watches, and one dreams — a Latvian version of the three smiths at the forge of the world. The giant rules the district with an iron staff, and Kurbads serves him to win his sister's hand, standing his tests at the mill, the forge, and the herd.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kurbads hero cycle as documented in Latvian collections; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the river the giant washes his staff and its strength washes away; Kurbads, warned by a friendly animal, fetches it out and finds the strength passes to whoever holds the wood. At the wrestling and the race of the giant's own rules Kurbads wins — and the three heads agree to give up their sister, for a man who can carry an oak under each arm and out-talk three heads at once is a bridegroom no Latvian father can refuse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the cycle; not verbatim.

title.en: Kurbads on the Eagle's Back: To the Sky-Maiden's Garden
title.zh: 鷹背上的庫爾巴德斯：天空少女的花園

region.en: Sky above Latvia (symbolic pin at Cesis)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞上空（象徵性定位於采西斯）

texts.period: Latvian hero cycle recorded 19th c.; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian collections

source.work: The Kurbads hero cycle, the Eagle-Flight episode; documented in Ruke-Dravina's Latvian tale collections

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain folk material; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Kurbads feeds the eagle whose nest he saved and rides its back to the sky — up past the clouds to the garden of the sky-maiden, where the sun's own daughter spins; he carries her back to earth to be his bride, and the flight home is long enough for the eagle to eat him a hundred years later.
summary.zh: 庫爾巴德斯曾救鷹巢並屢屢餵鷹；鷹載其背直上九霄——穿雲過霧，抵天空少女的花園，太陽親女正在彼處紡紗；他攜她返地為妻；歸途漫長，鷹中途饑而啄其肉，百年後他復得重生。

sensitivity.note: Ascension motif parallel to the daina's rose-tree climb.

passages.text: Kurbads has saved an eagle's nest and fed the young; the grown eagle offers to carry him into the sky on its back. Up past the clouds he rides, the cold thinning and the world shrinking beneath, until he comes to the garden of the sky-maiden — the golden garden where the sun's own daughter sits spinning the rays of morning into thread.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kurbads hero cycle as documented in Latvian collections; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sky-maiden is won and brought back to earth as Kurbads's bride; on the long flight home the eagle grows hungry, and Kurbads cuts pieces from his own body to feed her, in the oldest way of the flying tales. Years later the drops of blood he left in the sky grow into new flesh and the hero is restored — so that the Latvians say of Kurbads that he has been to the sky twice, once coming and once returning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the cycle; not verbatim.

title.en: Pilenai: The Fortress That Chose Death over Slavery
title.zh: 皮萊奈：寧死不為奴的堡壘

region.en: Pilenai fortress, Samogitia (symbolic pin at Pilenai)
region.zh: 薩莫吉提亞皮萊奈堡（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event dated 1336; recorded in the Rhymed Chronicle of Livonia (c. 1290-1340) and the Lithuanian chronicle tradition

source.work: The fall of Pilenai, from the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle and Lithuanian chronicle tradition; documented in Gimbutas, The Balts (1963)

texts.license: Scholarly documentation of public-domain chronicle; passages are paraphrase

summary.en: Besieged by the Teutonic Order, Duke Margiris's people of Pilenai gathered their treasure, burned the fortress, killed their own children and old folk, and threw themselves into the flames or on the swords rather than be taken — 'We will die free', said the chronicle, 'not live as slaves.'
summary.zh: 條頓騎士團圍皮萊奈堡，馬爾吉里斯公爵之民聚其財寶、焚其堡壘，親手終結孩童與老者之命，寧自投火海或迎利劍，不受俘——編年史云：『吾等寧為自由而死，不為奴而生。』

sensitivity.note: Mass suicide of a besieged garrison; treated as a national-legend of freedom, not endorsement.

passages.text: In 1336 the army of the Teutonic Order besieged Pilenai, the great hill-fortress of Samogitia under Duke Margiris. When the walls could no longer be held, the defenders took counsel and chose death over slavery: they burned their goods and their own houses, killed their children and their old folk with their own hands, and the men, women, and children who remained threw themselves into the flames or upon the swords of the enemy rather than be taken alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the fall of Pilenai as recorded in the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle and the Lithuanian chronicle tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chronicle tells it with horror and with admiration at once: of all the fortress only one man escaped, hidden in the reeds. In Lithuanian and Latvian memory Pilenai became the legend of freedom — the fortress that refused the yoke, whose defenders' death the Orders could never turn into a conquest; it stands in the national songs beside Laczplesis's fall as a name for resistance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the chronicle and its national reception; not verbatim.
